name: Meadowfoam seed oil

lead: Meadowfoam seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Limnanthes alba, a wildflower native to California and Oregon. It is used in creams, lip products and hair care as a light emollient that softens skin and adds shine.

Its fatty acids are mostly very long-chain types, which the sources link to its unusual resistance to going rancid. A 2021 cosmetic-science study tested it as a pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick; human skin-benefit trials were not found.

paras: People meet it as an ingredient in moisturisers, lipsticks and balms, hair serums and conditioners, or as a carrier oil. Its stability is a main reason formulators choose it, so it appears in long-shelf-life products.

Unpurified meadowfoam oil is not suitable for eating because of its high erucic acid. Topical safety data from clinical studies were not found. The plant's commercial crops have been vulnerable to fungal disease.

angle.text: Meadowfoam seed oil is a light, very oxidation-stable emollient used in creams, lip products and hair care. It softens skin and adds shine, and its stability is the main reason formulators use it.

lead: Meadowfoam seed oil is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of Limnanthes alba (white meadowfoam), an annual herb in the family Limnanthaceae native to wet grasslands, vernal pools and moist woodland in California and Oregon.[1] Formulators use it in skin-care, hair-care and colour cosmetics because it gives a soft, smooth skin feel and is very stable, which helps products look and feel good on skin, hair and lips.[1]

The seeds contain roughly 20 to 30 percent oil, which is made up of more than 98 percent long-chain fatty acids.[1] In cosmetics and hair care the oil is used for its emollient quality, soft skin feel and stability.[1] Published research on it is largely technical: a 2021 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science evaluated it as a natural pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick, compared with castor oil and octyldodecanol.[2]

No clinical studies of its effect on human skin or appearance as a single ingredient were found. It appears in a 2017 study of skin-barrier lipids only as one component of a natural-oil mixture used to make phytoceramides.[3]
infobox: Described as one of the most stable vegetable oils known[1]

paras: Reference sources give the main fatty acids of the oil as eicos-5-enoic acid (about 58-64 percent), docosa-5,13-dienoic acid (15-21 percent), erucic acid (10-14 percent) and docos-5-enoic acid (3-6 percent).[1] This long-chain profile is unusual among vegetable oils and is what separates it from most plant oils used in skin care, and it is reported to be most similar to rapeseed oil in composition.[1] Chemists have isolated individual meadowfoam fatty-acid esters, for example by silver-resin chromatography.[4]

The oil is described as among the most oxidatively stable vegetable oils known, which the source attributes mainly to its long-chain fatty acid content.[1] It can also be converted into waxes and lubricants.[1] A 2011 study reported that methyl esters of cold-pressed meadowfoam oil showed an exceptionally long induction period of 66.2 hours in fuel testing, compared with 5.9 and 4.5 hours for soybean and waste cooking oil esters, again pointing to oxidative stability.[5]

Meadowfoam oil appears in cosmetic and hair-care formulations for its emollient properties and skin feel.[1] Patent filings describe its use, alone or combined with hydrogenated jojoba oil, in lip glosses and eye liners and in personal-care compositions, and a Taiwanese patent describes it as a deposition enhancer for antioxidant vitamins in a cleansing composition.[6][7][8]

A 2021 laboratory study dispersed a red lake pigment at 20, 30 and 40 percent solid content in castor oil, octyldodecanol or meadowfoam oil and formulated several into lipsticks, which were tested for hardness, pay-off, friction, colour and four-week stability. Castor-oil dispersions were more viscous, stickier and harder to spread than the others, and all three oils wetted the pigment well.[2]

A 2017 study of phytoceramides used a mixture of macadamia nut, shea butter, moringa and meadowfoam seed oils as one of several natural-oil fatty-acid sources; the resulting ceramides improved recovery of damaged stratum corneum and hydration in human skin compared with a single C18 ceramide.[3] The study did not test meadowfoam oil alone.

Meadowfoam is grown on a small commercial scale. It is very susceptible to the fungus Botrytis cinerea, and commercial crops were devastated in the 1982 and 1984 growing seasons.[1] Unpurified oil is not considered suitable for human consumption, mainly because of its high erucic acid content.[1]

Meadowfoam oil comes from Limnanthes alba, white meadowfoam, a small annual wildflower of the meadowfoam family that is native to California and Oregon and grows in wet grassland, vernal pools and poorly drained soils. It has white cup-shaped flowers about one to one and a half centimetres across on stems reaching about 30 cm. [1] The seeds are roughly 20 to 30 percent oil. [1] Wikipedia notes that commercial crops were hit hard by the fungus Botrytis cinerea in 1982 and 1984. [1]

sections.h: Why it is used in skin and hair products
paras: The oil is unusually stable because more than 98 percent of it is long-chain fatty acids; the main constituents reported are eicosenoic acid (58 to 64 percent), docosadienoic acid (15 to 21 percent) and erucic acid (10 to 14 percent). [1] That stability gives it a long shelf life compared with many plant oils, and it is valued in cosmetics and hair care for an emollient, smooth, soft feel on skin. [1]

For appearance, the benefit people look for is a moisturising layer that leaves skin and hair smoother and softer. Patent literature describes its use in skin-care compositions with antioxidants and in blends with other seed oils. [6][7][5][8]

Meadowfoam oil can be converted into waxes and lubricants, a role similar to that once filled by whale oil, and honey from bees pollinating the crop is described as having a toasted-marshmallow flavour. [1] Unrefined seed oil is not considered suitable for eating because of its high erucic acid content. [1]

No studies found on meadowfoam seed oil alone in human skin. Existing published research concerns oil chemistry and cosmetic formulation, such as the lipstick pigment-dispersion study,[2] and one mixed-oil phytoceramide study in human skin.[3]

timeline.event: Commercial meadowfoam crops are devastated by Botrytis cinerea; another loss follows in 1984.[1]
A phytoceramide study uses a mixed oil including meadowfoam seed oil as a fatty-acid source.[3]
A study evaluates meadowfoam seed oil as a pigment dispersant in lipstick.[2]
